div.p: i've been continually dissatisfied with methods of bloggage on the static web. i've operated this blog page since the ass-end of my site's small history and its mock-backend has gone through far too many overhauls: from storing everything on one page to using iframes to pasting text into an html formatter to fetching from html fragment files... all the way to nearly writing my own markdown parser!? thankfully, at this point i stopped for a moment, considered, unearthed from my chest a great sigh of holiest resignment and turned to trek back down the hill of overcomplicated blogging solutions to good old iframes once more. and there i stayed, for some time.

why is it that my poor heart finds itself forever conflicted over—not what or why to write—but how to write?? writing freehand comes far more freely than writing within the labyrinths of syntax, yet labyrinthine syntax is the sole solution that offers the customizability i so enjoy. markdown—bless its heart—is incapable of floating images.

sami of the excellent podminton recently published a blog that extolled the virtues of a new blogging solution: neoblog, by scump. intrigued by the plosive power of its author's name, i investigated...!

content.p: neoblog is a yaml-based blogging system with which one defines an HTML template that is cloned and filled in based on the contents of a yaml file. it's a great system unfortunately obstructed by the fact that browsers don't support yaml and that its parser is 405 kilobytes in size.

i don't like my current blog setup. i store each blog entry as a separate html file and display them with an iframe, which means that every time i want to tweak the dom layout, i have to manually edit each file—which will only take longer and longer as i write more of these godawful things. introducing:
content.h3: the new setup & how to do it.
content.p: i'm moving from storing entries as html files to storing them as xml files. this means i can abstract a little ways up from the specific html structure and store data more concisely. however, i want to store entry content as html—which is very easy to do in xml (as opposed to something like yaml) because html is a close relative. minimal character backspacing necessary!

div.p: i'm not storing everything in one file like neoblog does. i have a set of buttons (to your left) with a data-entry attribute that display their associated entries on click. i just fetch the entry xml, feed it through a parser, fill in a template and plop the resulting elements into a wrapper div.

content.p: i've taken the opportunity to simplify my styling—this should mean less class-fiddling and more writing. hopefully the new system encourages me to write more. we'll see.
